title: Quasi-Newton updates: inverse Hessian
html:
\[\mathbf s_t=\mathbf x_{t+1}-\mathbf x_t,\quad\mathbf q_t=\mathbf g_{t+1}-\mathbf g_t,\quad r=(\mathbf q^\top\mathbf s)^{-1}.\]

Write \(\mathbf B,\mathbf A,\mathbf s,\mathbf q\) for the current quantities; \(\mathbf A\) approximates the inverse Hessian. Suppress the step index in the updates below.

BFGS
\((\mathbf I-r\mathbf s\mathbf q^\top)\mathbf A(\mathbf I-r\mathbf q\mathbf s^\top)+r\mathbf s\mathbf s^\top\)
Broyden
\(\mathbf A+\frac{(\mathbf s-\mathbf A\mathbf q)\mathbf s^\top\mathbf A}{\mathbf s^\top\mathbf A\mathbf q}\)
DFP
\(\mathbf A+\frac{\mathbf s\mathbf s^\top}{\mathbf s^\top\mathbf q}-\frac{\mathbf A\mathbf q\mathbf q^\top\mathbf A}{\mathbf q^\top\mathbf A\mathbf q}\)
SR1
\(\mathbf A+\frac{(\mathbf s-\mathbf A\mathbf q)(\mathbf s-\mathbf A\mathbf q)^\top}{(\mathbf s-\mathbf A\mathbf q)^\top\mathbf q}\)

All denominators must be nonzero. BFGS preserves positive definiteness under the curvature condition \(\mathbf q^\top\mathbf s>0\); Broyden’s general rank-one update need not preserve symmetry.

Symmetric Broyden class: \(\mathbf B_{t+1}=(1-\phi_t)\mathbf B_{t+1}^{\mathrm{BFGS}}+\phi_t\mathbf B_{t+1}^{\mathrm{DFP}},\quad\phi_t\in[0,1]\).

title: L-BFGS: limited memory
html:
• BFGS stores a dense \(\mathbf A_t\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}\): \(O(p^2)\) memory.
  • L-BFGS keeps only the latest \(m\) displacement–gradient pairs:
\[\mathbf s_i=\mathbf x_{i+1}-\mathbf x_i,\qquad\mathbf y_i=\nabla f(\mathbf x_{i+1})-\nabla f(\mathbf x_i).\]
  • Discard the oldest pair when the memory is full.
  • Compute \(\mathbf d_t=-\mathbf A_t\mathbf g_t\) without forming \(\mathbf A_t\).
Storage and direction computation: \(O(mp)\), with \(m\ll p\).
A_t is the inverse-Hessian approximation, consistent with the BFGS slides. Complexity excludes gradient evaluations and line search. Memory m counts correction pairs; p is parameter dimension.

title: L-BFGS: a low-rank correction
html:
• Store the latest \(m\) pairs \((\mathbf s_i,\mathbf y_i)\).
  • Approximate the inverse Hessian by a scaled identity plus a correction of rank at most \(2m\).
\(\mathbf A_t=\delta_t\mathbf I+\mathbf U_t\mathbf M_t\mathbf U_t^\top,\qquad\mathbf U_t\in\mathbb R^{p\times r},\quad r\le2m.\)

Search direction: \(\mathbf d_t=-\mathbf A_t\mathbf g_t\).
Storage and direction computation: \(O(mp)\).

Low-rank correction; generally full-rank \(\mathbf A_t\).

Conceptual compact representation of inverse L-BFGS. With m retained BFGS corrections, the difference from the positive scaled identity has rank at most 2m, bounded also by p. U is built from retained displacement and gradient information; M is a small symmetric core and need not be positive definite by itself. The full approximation remains positive definite under the usual curvature conditions. Actual direction computation normally uses the two-loop recursion; no explicit U/M factorization is required. Full recursion preserved in the prior source checkpoint and work/add-lbfgs-slides.py.

title: L-BFGS in practice
html:
• Useful for large, smooth problems when gradients are reliable and a dense BFGS matrix is too expensive.
  • Choose the step length \(\eta_t\) with a line search; Wolfe conditions support positive curvature pairs.
  • Skip or safeguard pairs when \(\mathbf s_i^\top\mathbf y_i\le0\).
  • Limited memory trades older curvature information for lower storage and computation.
  • For box constraints, use a suitable extension such as L-BFGS-B.

Curvature information from gradient differences.
Limited storage of the most recent correction pairs.

Classical deterministic L-BFGS is not automatically robust to noisy mini-batch curvature differences. L-BFGS-B is a distinct bound-constrained extension, not simple clipping of vanilla L-BFGS. No new trajectory is claimed here; the preceding animation remains full BFGS.

title: Newton, BFGS and L-BFGS in science
html:
ProblemNewton / Newton-typeBFGSL-BFGS
Likelihood fittingLogistic regression: likelihood Hessian or score equations.Smooth likelihoods with available gradients and costly Hessians.Many coefficients; retain a short history of gradient differences.
Scientific parameter estimationModel calibration with reliable second derivatives; Gauss–Newton for least squares.Fit ODE or physical-model parameters without second derivatives.Large inverse problems using adjoint gradients.
Molecular energy minimizationRefine structures near minima using energy curvature.Learn curvature from energies and forces.Relax large molecular systems with limited memory.

Newton also solves nonlinear equilibrium and discretized PDE equations, using the residual Jacobian rather than an objective Hessian.

Choose using derivative access, dimension and memory. For nonconvex objectives these are local methods; safeguards matter.

Examples illustrate suitable applications, not claims that every software package uses the same optimizer. Newton root finding solves J_R d = -R; optimization applies it to R = gradient f. Gauss–Newton approximates a nonlinear least-squares Hessian and is distinct from exact Newton. Large PDE problems often use matrix-free Newton–Krylov, so dense Newton storage is not universal.

title: From Adam to AdamW
html:
Keep Adam’s loss-gradient moments and bias correction:

\[\mathbf a_t=\frac{\widehat{\mathbf m}_t}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbf v}_t}+\epsilon_A}.\]

Adam

\[\mathbf x_t=\mathbf x_{t-1}-\eta_t\mathbf a_t.\]

AdamW also shrinks the previous parameters by \(1-\eta_t\lambda_{\rm wd}\).

\[\mathbf x_t=(1-\eta_t\lambda_{\rm wd})\mathbf x_{t-1}-\eta_t\mathbf a_t.\]

The decay is separate from the adaptive gradient step.
notes: Tutorial comparison: plain Adam versus AdamW. Both use only the sampled loss gradient in their moments. AdamW applies the separate factor 1-eta_t lambda_wd to previous parameters. title: Adam and AdamW: the recursions
html:
In each column, \(\mathbf g_t=\widehat{ abla f}(\mathbf x_{t-1})\). Start with zero moments; \(t\ge1\).

Adam

\[\mathbf g_t=\widehat{ abla f}(\mathbf x_{t-1})\]
\[\mathbf m_t= eta_1\mathbf m_{t-1}+(1- eta_1)\mathbf g_t\]
\[\mathbf v_t= eta_2\mathbf v_{t-1}+(1- eta_2)\mathbf g_t^{\odot2}\]
\[\widehat{\mathbf m}_t= rac{\mathbf m_t}{1- eta_1^t},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf v}_t= rac{\mathbf v_t}{1- eta_2^t}\]
\[\mathbf x_t=\mathbf x_{t-1}-\eta_t rac{\widehat{\mathbf m}_t}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbf v}_t}+\epsilon_A}\]

Apply the adaptive gradient step.

AdamW: decoupled weight decay

\[\mathbf g_t=\widehat{ abla f}(\mathbf x_{t-1})\]
\[\mathbf m_t= eta_1\mathbf m_{t-1}+(1- eta_1)\mathbf g_t\]
\[\mathbf v_t= eta_2\mathbf v_{t-1}+(1- eta_2)\mathbf g_t^{\odot2}\]
\[\widehat{\mathbf m}_t= rac{\mathbf m_t}{1- eta_1^t},\qquad\widehat{\mathbf v}_t= rac{\mathbf v_t}{1- eta_2^t}\]
\[ egin{aligned}\mathbf x_t={}&(1-\eta_t\lambda_{ m wd})\mathbf x_{t-1}\&-\eta_t rac{\widehat{\mathbf m}_t}{\sqrt{\widehat{\mathbf v}_t}+\epsilon_A}.\end{aligned}\]

Apply the same rule, with separate decay.

The moment rules are identical. Setting \(\lambda_{ m wd}=0\) recovers Adam. All operations are coordinatewise.

title: Constructing an iterative scheme
html:
One possible iterative scheme

1. Sample and evaluate

Maintain a search state \(S_t\) and draw \(q_t\) candidates from its sampling distribution \(P_t\):

\[\mathbf x^{(t,r)}\sim P_t,\quad y_{t,r}=f(\mathbf x^{(t,r)}),\qquad r=1,\ldots,q_t.\]

title: Constructing an iterative scheme
html:
One possible iterative scheme

1. Sample and evaluate

Maintain a search state \(S_t\) and draw \(q_t\) candidates from its sampling distribution \(P_t\):

\[\mathbf x^{(t,r)}\sim P_t,\quad y_{t,r}=f(\mathbf x^{(t,r)}),\qquad r=1,\ldots,q_t.\]

2. Select

Compare the evaluated candidates. Keep useful candidates or rank them:

\[y_{t,(1)}\leq\cdots\leq y_{t,(q_t)}.\]

For example: accept an improving candidate, or select several highly ranked candidates.

title: What is optimization?
html:
Choose feasible decisions to make a specified objective as good as possible.

\[\min_{\mathbf x\in\mathcal X} f(\mathbf x),\qquad \mathcal X\subseteq\mathbb R^p.\]
  • Decisions: \(\mathbf x\) contains the quantities we can change.
  • Objective: \(f(\mathbf x)\) measures loss, cost or energy; here, smaller is better.
  • Constraints: \(\mathcal X\) contains the allowed choices.

In practice: find a good solution within the available time, evaluations and memory.

Bridge from the quoted definitions to the course notation. We write minimization throughout; maximizing a score is equivalent to minimizing its negative. The formulation does not assume the infimum is attained. The landscape is the objective viewed over the decision space. Ask for participants' own examples on the following original slide. Do not replace or remove that discussion.

title: Muon: the polar update direction
html:
One matrix block; \(\mathbf G_t=\nabla_{\mathbf W}f_t(\mathbf W_{t-1})\), \(\mathbf M_0=0\).

\[\mathbf M_t=\beta\mathbf M_{t-1}+(1-\beta)\mathbf G_t,\qquad\mathbf M_t=\mathbf U_t\mathbf\Sigma_t\mathbf V_t^\top.\]
\[\mathbf P_t=\mathbf U_t\mathbf V_t^\top,\qquad\mathbf W_t=\mathbf W_{t-1}-\eta_t\mathbf P_t.\]

Teaching variant: plain momentum and exact polar factor; omit decay and shape scaling.

What changes when all nonzero singular values become 1?

html:

\[\mathbf P_t=\mathbf U_t\mathbf V_t^\top,\qquad\mathbf W_t=\mathbf W_{t-1}-\eta_t\mathbf P_t.\]

title: Polar Express: computing the direction
html:
Approximate the polar factor using matrix products, without an SVD at each update.

\[\mathbf X_{j+1}=a_j\mathbf X_j+b_j(\mathbf X_j\mathbf X_j^\top)\mathbf X_j+c_j(\mathbf X_j\mathbf X_j^\top)^2\mathbf X_j.\]
\[s_{j+1}=a_js_j+b_js_j^3+c_js_j^5,\qquad\text{target }s=1\quad(s_0>0).\]

Polar Express chooses a new polynomial for each inner iteration, using a spectral interval.

Start with \(\mathbf X_0=\mathbf M_t/(1.01\|\mathbf M_t\|_{\rm F}+\epsilon_P)\).

How can a scalar polynomial transform an entire matrix spectrum?

The classical cubic uses fixed coefficients; Polar Express adapts its quintic coefficients.

\[\mathbf X_{j+1}=a_j\mathbf X_j+b_j(\mathbf X_j\mathbf X_j^\top)\mathbf X_j+c_j(\mathbf X_j\mathbf X_j^\top)^2\mathbf X_j.\]
\[s_{j+1}=a_js_j+b_js_j^3+c_js_j^5,\qquad\text{target }s=1\quad(s_0>0).\]

title: Landscape features from samples
html:
DIRECT and Bayesian optimization are useful when the dimension and evaluation budget permit.
In higher dimensions, what can a first sample
tell us about the landscape?
Estimate useful characteristics of the function,
then use what we learn to guide further search.
This is the role of landscape fingerprints: approximate sample-based characteristics, not a complete reconstruction. The distinction is practical rather than a hard dimensional cutoff. Estimation itself consumes evaluations and carries uncertainty.

title: Parallel searches and restarts
html:
Explore more than one basin.

  • Run several searches from different starting points.
  • Or restart a search with a new initialization.
  • Share the total evaluation budget across runs; compare their best observed values.

Parallel runs can reduce wall-clock time when resources are available. They still consume evaluations.

Close the chapter by reconnecting sampling and adaptation to multi-funnel structure. Independent restarts and parallel runs need not exchange information. Neither finite restarts nor several populations guarantee global optimality. Compare under a shared total evaluation budget; distinguish total evaluations from elapsed time. title: Gradient and curvature
html:
• The gradient of the function is available.
  • The function can be high-dimensional.
  • Higher-order information may also be available.
\(f(\mathbf x)=(1-x_1)^2+100(x_2-x_1^2)^2,\qquad \mathbf x\in\mathbb R^2.\)

Gradient: local slope

\[ abla f(\mathbf x)= egin{pmatrix} rac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}\[3pt] rac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}\end{pmatrix}= egin{pmatrix}2(x_1-1)-400x_1(x_2-x_1^2)\200(x_2-x_1^2)\end{pmatrix}.\]

\(- abla f(\mathbf x)\): steepest local decrease.

\(f(\mathbf x+\mathbf s)\approx f(\mathbf x)+ abla f(\mathbf x)^ op\mathbf s+ frac12\mathbf s^ op\mathbf H(\mathbf x)\mathbf s.\)

title: Gradient and curvature
html:
• The gradient of the function is available.
  • The function can be high-dimensional.
  • Higher-order information may also be available.
\(f(\mathbf x)=(1-x_1)^2+100(x_2-x_1^2)^2,\qquad \mathbf x\in\mathbb R^2.\)

Hessian: local curvature

\[\mathbf H(\mathbf x)=\nabla^2f(\mathbf x)=\left[\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\right]_{i,j=1}^2\]\[=\begin{pmatrix}1200x_1^2-400x_2+2&-400x_1\\-400x_1&200\end{pmatrix}.\]
At \(\mathbf x=(-0.8,\,0.5)^\top\):\[\mathbf H(\mathbf x)=\begin{pmatrix}570&320\\320&200\end{pmatrix}.\]

Eigenvectors: principal directions.
Eigenvalues: curvature in these directions.

\(f(\mathbf x+\mathbf s)\approx f(\mathbf x)+\nabla f(\mathbf x)^\top\mathbf s+\tfrac12\mathbf s^\top\mathbf H(\mathbf x)\mathbf s.\)

title: Strong convexity: contraction in one step
html:
Assume convexity, \(L\)-smoothness and \(\mu\)-strong convexity.
Choose \(\eta=1/L;\) keep the same \(e_t,D_t,R\).

1. Expand the squared distance
\[D_{t+1}=D_t-2\eta\mathbf g_t^\top(\mathbf x_t-\mathbf x^\star)+\eta^2\|\mathbf g_t\|_2^2.\]
2. Use strong convexity
\[f(\mathbf x^\star)\ge f(\mathbf x_t)+\mathbf g_t^\top(\mathbf x^\star-\mathbf x_t)+\tfrac\mu2\|\mathbf x^\star-\mathbf x_t\|_2^2.\]
\[\begin{aligned}\mathbf g_t^\top(\mathbf x_t-\mathbf x^\star)&\ge e_t+\tfrac\mu2D_t,\\[5pt]D_{t+1}&\le(1-\mu\eta)D_t-2\eta e_t+\eta^2\|\mathbf g_t\|_2^2.\end{aligned}\]
3. Use smoothness
\[\begin{aligned}\eta^2\|\mathbf g_t\|_2^2&\le2\eta(e_t-e_{t+1}),\\ -2\eta e_t+\eta^2\|\mathbf g_t\|_2^2&\le-2\eta e_{t+1}\le0.\end{aligned}\]
\(\boxed{D_{t+1}\le(1-\mu/L)D_t.}\)

title: Adaptive step sizes
html:
• So far, we chose a constant step size using assumptions about the function.
  • We can instead choose a step size \(\eta_t\) at each iteration:
\[\mathbf x_{t+1}=\mathbf x_t-\eta_t\mathbf g_t,\qquad\mathbf g_t=\nabla f(\mathbf x_t).\]
  • A schedule specifies \(\eta_t\) in advance, for example a decreasing sequence.
  • An adaptive rule uses information from the current iteration, such as function values or the gradient.
  • Line search tests candidate step sizes. The Polyak rule uses the objective error and gradient norm.

Here \(\eta_t\) is one scalar for the whole gradient.
